brief.head: Gods of the gaps
brief.text: Early humans filled what they could not explain with sun gods and wind gods, Amit Varma said. Some questions stay unanswered, but that does not make God the answer. {083-C05}

brief.head: Four bins for beliefs
brief.text: Ajay Shah sorts beliefs into four bins, from untestable nonsense to hard knowledge. In between sit unproven working bets: if you hold some, “Welcome aboard.” {083-C03}

brief.head: Armies of the faithful
brief.text: Bands of hunter-gatherers averaged 150 people, Ajay Shah said. Religion let far bigger groups fight as fanatics for an invisible cause, and bigger armies won. {083-C10}

brief.head: Wired to care
brief.text: Compassion and family love are genuine feelings that evolved because they helped our genes spread, Amit Varma said. A selfish gene does not make us selfish: “We’re hardwired to love.” {083-C07}

brief.head: Light, without belief
brief.text: Refusing to celebrate Diwali because you don’t believe in Hinduism makes no sense, Amit Varma said, when family gathers and there is light everywhere. {083-C15}

thought.text: I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.
thought.who: Douglas Adams on natural selection, as Amit Varma read it out on the gods of the gaps

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on life without religion
lead.head: In no God we trust
body: All over the world, religiosity has been going down, Ajay Shah said as he opened the episode. So what happens to people “when they choose to walk out of the operating system of religion”?
Both hosts are atheists, and for Amit Varma the subject was personal.
Atheists across the world are frowned upon and even treated with anger, he said. In 13 countries, atheism or public apostasy can be punished by death. {#thirteen}
Varma’s own test of social progress is not a woman president of the United States. “What I would love to see is, say, a gay atheist in the White House,” he said.
## Not a belief

He began with the word. The “ism” in atheism suggests a belief system, Varma said, and so people assume that atheists believe there is no God. “The correct definition involves not belief but an absence of belief.” {083-C01}

No one has proved to him that God exists, any more than pink fairies, so he believes in neither. “I believe that there is no God” claims a false certainty, he argued, since no one can prove a negative.
The burden of proof lies with whoever makes the claim. If anyone proved that God exists, Varma said, he would become a believer: “I’m a rationalist. I go by the proof.”
Nor is an agnostic a fence-sitter between believer and atheist. Atheism is about belief and agnosticism about knowledge, Varma said, and he is both an atheist and an agnostic.
## What faith was for

None of this denies religion’s past. It has played “a superbly important role through human history”, Varma said, and he listed the four functions it has served: explanation, meaning, morality and consolation.
Science has filled most of the gaps that gods once explained. Meaning, he argued, has to come from reality, not from “manufactured fiction”. {083-C04}
Morality, in his account, came before religion. Evolution wired in compassion, living together produced norms, and religion arrived last to codify them.
Consolation in the face of death was the one job he conceded. Still, he would not believe in a fiction to console himself. “Grief is grief,” he said.
## Faith in retreat
Shah took the long view. Household surveys show religiosity declining all over the world: first in Western Europe after the Second World War, and over the last 25 years in the United States as well.

His explanation is that every religion looks strange to those not raised in it. Faith that is not “dinned into your head as a child” rarely takes, so a family that leaves does not return. “So it’s like once it’s gone, it can never come back.” {083-C12}
Conformity speeds the process. When most people are religious, the rest go along; once belief falls below a critical mass, people start saying openly that they don’t care.
Shah suggested that, with right-wing religious nationalism on the rise, harmful old beliefs may need calling out more firmly.
Varma ended with three exhortations: beware the new secular religions, keep the traditions that bring people together, and never impose your beliefs on anyone.

Atheists who mock believers behave badly too, he said, and many of his friends are religious. “I think the greatest religion is to treat other human beings as actual people and not as means to an end.” {083-C16}

second.label: Defining atheism
second.head: No stamps, no church
second.deck: Amit Varma reads out a reader’s letter to The Economist in full
body: In 2007, when Amit Varma wrote the first of his columns on atheism, *The Economist* had called atheism a new religion. A reader, Chad English of Ottawa, wrote in to protest, and Varma read his letter out in full. {#economist}

Why don’t atheists organise or wield influence? “The answer is easy,” English wrote. “Atheism is a religion in the same way that not collecting stamps is a hobby.” A government that pushed laws favouring stamp collecting would be a bad government, he added, and the same is true of a religious one.
Then the sign-off: “See you at the next non-meeting.” Varma borrows the comparison whenever someone calls atheism another religion or a belief system. {083-S02}

quote.text: Atheism is no more a religion than not collecting stamps is a hobby.

second.caption: the letter from Ottawa

third.head: Survival of the cutest
body: Why did the sun god and the wind god last? Ajay Shah passed on an insight from Ashok Desai, who told him that the human mind came first. {#desai}

In the oral tradition, Desai said, people kept inventing and mutating stories. The fanciful ones that were cute and interesting to the human mind stuck; the ones that clicked inside the brain were remembered.
Shah gave the idea a modern form. “There are fifty thousand subreddits about the murder of JFK, and a couple of them gain prominence because they just fit in the human mind better.” {083-S05}
On this account, the stories that survive are those that fit the mind best. Shah offered it in response to Amit Varma’s account of the gods of the gaps.
third.caption: the stories that stuck

p2.title: The atheist’s case
p2.deck: Amit Varma on what atheism is, what religion does, and how to live without it; Ajay Shah on faith’s decline

sections.label: The definition
sections.head: Absence makes the case
sections.caption: atheism as an absence of belief
body: Atheism is misunderstood by many people, Amit Varma said, and he wanted to define it first. The trouble begins with the word. Its “ism” suggests a belief system, so people think of atheists as people who believe that there is no God.
That, he said, is not the correct definition. “The correct definition involves not belief but an absence of belief.” {083-C01}

No one has proved to him that God exists, so he does not believe in God, just as he does not believe in pink fairies. “I believe that there is no God” claims a false certainty, he said, because no one can prove a negative. “I don’t believe that there is God” is in an entirely different category.
## The burden of proof
The burden of proof lies with the person who says “I believe X”, Varma said, not with him. If someone proved tomorrow that God exists, he would become a believer: he goes by the proof.

Nor is atheism an activity. “It is a passive thing,” he said. A reader’s letter to *The Economist*, from around the time of Varma’s first columns on atheism in 2007, made the point with stamps. {#economist}
~ Varma is not militant about it. Many of his friends are religious, and that is perfectly fine with him: “Let’s not impose on each other.”

quote.text: If someone were to hypothetically prove tomorrow that God does exist, then I will be a believer because I’m a rationalist.

sections.label: Two questions
sections.head: Knowing is not believing
sections.caption: belief, knowledge and four bins
body: People picture belief as a line, Amit Varma said: the believer at one end, the atheist at the other, and the undecided agnostic in the middle. That is not true. “Atheism is about belief. Agnostic is about knowledge.” {083-C02}
The root of agnostic is *gnosis*, knowledge. An agnostic holds that the truth about God can never be known. So a believer can be an agnostic, and so, like Varma, can an atheist.
## Four bins
Ajay Shah connected this to Karl Popper. A theory is interesting and worth considering, he said, when it makes predictions that are vulnerable to falsification. {083-R12}

From that he built a set of bins. At one edge sits fanciful nonsense like Erich von Däniken’s *Chariots of the Gods*, which Shah read as a child and which “just doesn’t make a single testable proposition”. {083-J10} At the other is hard knowledge such as evolutionary biology. In between are working bets that future evidence may settle, and beliefs held because of social programming, peer pressure or convenience.

~ Everybody holds beliefs of that last kind, Shah said, and it would be good to be self-aware about them. As for the middle zone: “So, gentle reader, if you’re embarrassed to believe some things that you’re not yet ready to prove, great. Welcome aboard.” {083-C03}

quote.text: Equally, like me, you can be an atheist and an agnostic at the same time.

sections.label: What religion does
sections.head: Four jobs, one vacancy
sections.caption: the four jobs religion does
body: Atheists are often asked what could replace religion, Amit Varma said. He named four functions it performs, and confessed that for one of them he had no convincing answer. {#functions}

The first is explanation. Early humans made up a sun god and a wind god, and as knowledge filled the gaps, those gods of the gaps vanished. Varma read out Douglas Adams: “I take the awe of understanding over the awe of ignorance any day.” {083-J07}
The second is meaning, which must come from reality, he said, or it would be “fake and shallow”.
## Goodness before God

The third is morality. Evolution wired in compassion and care for kin, living together produced norms such as not stealing, and religion came last to codify them. “First we have the hardwiring, then people live together, then you have the norms, then religion kind of codifies it.” {083-C06}

Reason does the rest. Plato’s Euthyphro dilemma asks whether something is good because God wills it, or whether God wills it because it is good; either way, morality does not depend on God. {083-C08} Kant, Bentham and Mill, and Aristotle each reached ethics without religion.
~ The fourth is consolation in the face of death, and there Varma concedes ground. “I can’t help being an atheist,” he said. {083-S03}

quote.text: God could go mad one day and will any damn thing and we have to do it.

sections.label: New atheism
sections.head: When atheism got loud
sections.caption: the Four Horsemen of new atheism
body: The atheism Ajay Shah and Amit Varma grew up with was personal and benign. Shah’s father was an atheist who blended easily into a religious society. But Shah sees a more hawkish atheistic culture shaping up.

About twenty years ago, Varma said, a group of people came to believe, “if I may say so with good reason”, that religion is a root cause of much evil in the world, and that they must speak out. {#twentyyears}

They became the Four Horsemen: Richard Dawkins, author of *The God Delusion*; Sam Harris, author of *The End of Faith*; Daniel Dennett; and Christopher Hitchens, whom Varma adored and still misses. {083-R03}

Dawkins called the God of the Old Testament “arguably the most unpleasant character in all fiction”. {#oldtestament} He also pointed out that every believer is an atheist about all the other religions. {083-C11}
## A movement played out

The irony, Varma said, is that their assertiveness made atheism look like just another competing belief system. He agrees with many of their critiques of organised religion and dogma, but feels religions encode traditions that exist for a reason.
~ The movement has played itself out, he said. Two of the four horsemen, Dennett and Hitchens, are dead, and Dawkins is in his eighties. {#twodead}

quote.text: Dawkins beautifully pointed out that actually every believer is an atheist because you believe in your one religion.

portraits.hint: writer, one of the Four Horsemen

sections.label: Faith in decline
sections.head: Below the critical mass
sections.caption: why religiosity keeps falling
body: Household surveys show religiosity falling worldwide, Ajay Shah said. In Western Europe it fell after the Second World War. As the famous quote goes, “After Auschwitz, there can be no art”; after it, faith in a benign, all-powerful God was hard to hold. {083-J09}
In the United States it held up for a while, then collapsed over the last 25 years.
Shah’s reason the decline is irreversible: to anyone not raised in a faith, its beliefs sound weird. Once a family stops passing faith on, he said, “it can never come back”. {083-C12}
## Tipping points

Conformity matters too. When religiosity was 60, 70, 80 per cent, people had a strong reason to go along; below some critical mass, they start saying openly that they don’t care, and the decline accelerates. {#critical}

Amit Varma recalled Hannah Arendt’s “banality of evil”: ordinary people can show the greatest cruelty, and neither religion nor rationality guards against it. Prosperity, he suggested, makes it least likely: “perhaps the best answer to get to the kind of morality we would all like is a rising GDP”. {083-C13}

~ Shah offered a counterexample: Nazi Germany, “the land of Albert Einstein and Beethoven”. {#einstein} Varma replied that it rose from the ruins of the First World War, without which he doubted Hitler would have come to power.

quote.text: My sisters and I have zero. Their kids have zero.

sections.label: Closing thoughts
sections.head: Keep the lamps, drop the dogma
sections.caption: keeping tradition without dogma
body: Amit Varma closed with three exhortations. The first: organised religion is declining, but the instinct to choose a belief system is still there, in new religions from Marxism to wokeism, each with its own dogma and intolerance.
Question any part of the woke dogma, he said, and you are an outcast; support an outcast and you become one too. It reminded him of Pakistan’s blasphemy law: “And turtles all the way down.” {083-J11}
Anyone who accepts an ideological tribe’s entire package, Varma said, is not thinking independently. {083-C14}
## Baby and bathwater

The second: don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater. Traditions give comfort and community. As for refusing to celebrate Diwali because you don’t believe in Hinduism, he sees no sense in it. “You don’t need to believe in God to celebrate a tradition like that.” {083-C15}
Keep away the regressive, misogynistic customs, he said, embrace the life-affirming ones, and never coerce anyone.
~ The third: whether you are religious or an atheist, don’t impose your beliefs on others. Atheists who mock believers behave badly too. {083-C16}

quote.text: But there are some things that can be life affirming, that can bring you closer to your fellow people, embrace them.

side.boxText: Richard Dawkins wrote *The Selfish Gene*, which Amit Varma says is widely misread: selfish genes make us loving, not selfish. He also wrote *The God Delusion*, and pointed out that every believer is an atheist about all the other religions. {083-C11}

contQuote.text: So whenever anyone conforms to the entire belief package of some ideological tribe, I know they’re not thinking independently for themselves. And they might just be a devout bhakta of whatever ideological tribe that is.

p3.deck: Spaghetti, grief, a father’s exit and a teenage detour, and what each teaches

stories.caption: the Flying Spaghetti Monster
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the gentlest way to protest religion
stories.head: Hands off my spaghetti
body: Amit Varma’s favourite protest against religion is a benign one, and it started in Kansas. In 2005, the Kansas School Board was trying to teach creationism, and a gentleman named Bobby Henderson wrote it a letter. {#kansas}
If the board was going to treat all beliefs equally, Henderson argued, it would have to treat his too. He believed in Pastafarianism, whose followers worship the Flying Spaghetti Monster.
And if other religions were not to be offended, Varma said, voicing Henderson, then neither was he: “The Flying Spaghetti Monster is my God. I’m a proud Pastafarian.”
Around 2007, Varma took up Henderson’s creation in a column about free speech called *Don’t Insult Pasta*. He, too, declared himself a Pastafarian. {083-S04}
The satirical point was simple. “If you don’t want me to offend your God, don’t offend mine,” he said. “Say nothing about pasta.”

It was all tongue in cheek, Varma added, before swerving into diet advice. Pasta is carbs, he warned, and readers should eat a lot of meat, some fat and not much carb. Pasta is evil, except once in a while. {083-J03}
Even here he would not lay down the law. He was not going to be dogmatic about it, he said, because good atheists are not dogmatic.
~ He likes this tongue-in-cheek way of doing things, he said, because it makes the absurdity of others visible. It is gentler than the new atheists, who spoke out against religion very strongly.
stories.why: Demands for special treatment, and for beliefs never to be offended, look arbitrary once anyone can found a faith. Gentle satire exposes that without hostility, which is why Varma prefers it to the assertiveness of new atheism. {083-R11}

stories.start: I remember when my mother died in two thousand and seven, I wrote
stories.end: but then I don't have an option. This is just how I am.
stories.caption: consolation for an atheist
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the one thing reason cannot give
stories.head: Comfort he would not fake
body: Amit Varma’s mother died in 2007. The next year he wrote a column in *Mail Today* called *What’s Consolation for an Atheist?* {083-R08}

It took on the one function of religion he admits he cannot replace. Explanation, meaning and morality can come from science and reason, he argued, but mortality is hard to deal with, and on consolation he has no answer.
The conclusion he reached then still holds. “I can’t help being an atheist. I’m not going to start believing in a fiction because I need to console myself.” {083-S03}

~ Varma doubts religion offers much comfort either. “Ultimately bereavement is bereavement, grief is grief,” he said. If he concedes any ground to religion, it is here, “but then I don’t have an option”.
stories.why: Intellectual honesty can cost comfort. Rather than pretend that reason solves everything, Varma openly gives up this one piece of ground to religion, and still declines to believe in a consoling fiction.

stories.start: So it's like my father switched out of deep commitment to Hinduism
stories.end: My sisters and I have zero. Their kids have zero. And so on.
stories.caption: his father’s exit from Hinduism
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a family that left religion for good
stories.head: The family that never went back
body: As a young person, Ajay Shah’s father had a deep commitment to Hinduism and a deep knowledge of it. As an adult, he became an atheist. {083-S06}
His atheism was relaxed. “My father was atheist, but it was never uncomfortable,” Shah said. He blended perfectly into a society with many religious people, as Shah does today.
After the switch, religion vanished from the family. “My sisters and I have zero. Their kids have zero.” And, Shah said, “once it’s gone, it can never come back”. {083-C12}

~ Shah told the story while explaining why religiosity is falling worldwide. To anyone not raised in a faith, he said, its beliefs sound weird, just as the Christians’ beliefs would to someone raised a Buddhist.
stories.why: The story is Shah’s larger thesis in miniature. Belief that is not instilled in childhood rarely returns, he argues, so a family that leaves religion stays out, and the decline of religiosity runs in one direction.

stories.start: there was a vague time in my teens when I was very immature
stories.end: But I started thinking about atheism seriously as an adult.
stories.caption: his teenage spirituality
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how he reasoned his way out
stories.head: The spirit was willing, briefly
body: Amit Varma says he was always an atheist. But there was a vague time in his teens, when he was “very immature”, when he held that spirituality was different from religion.
In that phase he believed there was “some vast unknowable presence which governs us all”. Then, he said, “I was soon disabused of that notion by life and rationality.” {083-S01}
Many people turn to atheism as an act of rebellion against convention. Varma said he did not really do that, though it might have been part of the story.

~ He began to think about atheism seriously only as an adult, and arrived at his definition of it over a long period. That definition, an absence of belief rather than a belief, became the starting point of the episode. {083-C01}
stories.why: Disbelief can be reasoned into slowly rather than seized in a single act of rebellion. For Varma, a spirituality distinct from religion was a halfway house he soon left behind.
